From the archives: "Making Sense of the Ambivalent Politics of Deportation Defense Campaigns." This was one of my earliest Substack posts from 2021, but remains relevant today. 

austinkocher.substack.com/p/…

Terrifying. Everything conservatives legitimately fear about big government, and they are enabling the whole thing. Stand by your values, reject the cult of personality.


Freedom of the Press Foundation (@FreedomofPress)

The Trump administration is working to create a database of intimate details about every U.S. resident, which is "a giant honeypot for bad actors," @FreedomofPress's Lauren Harper told 1A.

If breached, it could cause an "identity theft nightmare."

Listen:the1a.org/segments/i
In a single recent month, ICE posted just 2 competitive contracts on SAM.gov and awarded at least 10 sole-source contracts, half justified by claiming 'only one responsible source exists.'

Federal law requires competitive bidding when the government buys goods or services above a certain threshold. It's how taxpayers get fair prices and accountability. ICE is increasingly bypassing this.
ICE has $150B+ in unspent enforcement funds and is racing to spend it by quietly bending federal procurement rules in three ways most people have never heard of. A thread.

Last thing. Raising $$ for my (soft-funded) academic research + my public work is actually super difficult. My work could go away, it's not guaranteed. So if you do value it, consider a paid sub austinkocher.substack.com/su… or help connect me to larger foundation funding. 🙏

I am def not discouraging outreach to me. I welcome it. But to make sure that this work is sustainable over the next three years of the Trump admin and beyond, I need help raising the quality of our conversations from vague to precise. Many of you already rock at this.

Re: doing more analysis, I totally understand the request - but I get lots of these. That's why I created Relevant Research w/ Adam Sawyer & Riwaj Chalise, so we can quickly handle research Qs under a very affordable yet sustainable business model. -> adam@relevant-research.com

Trust me: I know there are lots of real Qs! 

This approach is in our mutual self-interest: it's the best way to ensure you get a response and that I can respond quickly and helpfully. Even better, post the question in the comments of the post so that everyone can learn!

If you do need to reach out with questions, it is enormously helpful if you could pause before you hit send, make sure you read the article (+ back articles if related), and use your reading to identify the precise thing you need from me that genuinely isn't clearly elucidated.

Please don't misunderstand me: I am deeply honored for the attention that this work gets. But every minute I spend trying to decipher a vague request or explaining something I've already explained, it takes away from other work and other people who need support, too.

Given how much time I spend writing careful posts, a general or imprecise request feels like I'm being asked to re-explain something I've already explained and spend additional time doing it that has to come from somewhere. (I already work insane hours.)

However, I also get a lot of Qs that are basically, "can you talk about your post?" or "can you explain your post?" or "can you do more analysis for me?" 

Again, nothing wrong with this, but I need to gently flag this as an issue and request some thoughtfulness and generosity.

This is sort of a double-edge sword in the sense: I hope my writing answers Qs for a broader audience (rather than answering Qs 1-on-1), but it also naturally generates more Qs. That's understandable, welcome, part of the knowledge cycle. I'm honored that so many people engage.

I write frequently at austinkocher.substack.com. That's by far the best outlet for my work right now. The work is entirely unpaywalled under the NPR model. No one has to pay for it (though it's great if you can support it.) I provide analysis, graphs, links, footnotes, sources, etc

I need to share a quick housekeeping note about the public work I do to try to support immigration data analysis for the whole community. I draw on my years of experience to write quickly, precisely, & helpfully, w/ as much documentation as I can to help folks understand data.

ICE Is Violating Its Own Family Separation Policies

Zain Lakhani explains how the United States is creating a long-term family separation crisis that will last for decades and why we urgently need to build an international family reunification system.

austinkocher.substack.com/p/…

Protection should not depend on political cycles. The U.S. must extend TPS or build a durable pathway not dismantle a lifeline that tens of thousands of families have built their lives around. 

Read: theimmigrationlab.org/blog/f…

Even without institutions, Honduran communities resist. Feminist artists like Dolls Clan turn public walls into memorials for femicide victims. Art preserves what policy abandons but art cannot replace protection.
The ACLU, National TPS Alliance, and immigrant-rights groups have filed a federal challenge calling the termination 'arbitrary and capricious' a reversal of a 25-year protection promise.

From the archives: "Making Sense of the Ambivalent Politics of Deportation Defense Campaigns." This was one of my earliest Substack posts from 2021, but remains relevant today. 

austinkocher.substack.com/p/making-sen...

Each of these actions may be technically legal. But together they form a pattern: billions in public money, moving fast, in the dark. 

Read: www.projectsaltbox.com/p/analysis-i... 
My substack: austinkocher.substack.com
MD, MI, and NJ have all sued DHS. Each argues ICE skipped required environmental review, community engagement, and alternatives analysis treating narrow legal exceptions as routine procedure.
The Romulus, MI site is within a mile of an elementary school and sits on a flood-prone lot. Michigan's lawsuit says federal officials never communicated with local leaders before moving forward.
On real property: ICE signed a $102M deed for the Williamsport warehouse just 4 days after initiating required historic preservation review without waiting for any response from the state.
Senators Warren and Shaheen wrote to Sec. Hegseth: 'DoD should not be allowing DHS to use WEXMAC to bypass federal acquisition procedures.' Hegseth has until April 13 to respond.

Two warehouse conversion contracts ($641M in Williamsport, MD and $704M in Surprise, AZ) were awarded through WEXMAC. The public and Congress have almost no visibility into the details of either deal.
GEO Group (one of the largest private prison companies in the country)was added to WEXMAC in January 2026. ICE is now using this military contract to build domestic immigration detention facilities.
Then there's WEXMAC TITUS, a Navy contract vehicle originally built for overseas military logistics. Last year it was quietly modified: scope expanded to the U.S., ceiling raised 550% to $65 billion.
ICE's justification? That the facility's 'proprietary infrastructure' (generators, housing units, food service equipment) means no one else could run it. Legal scholars and watchdogs are skeptical.
One of those sole-source awards: a $1.2B contract to Amentum Services to manage Camp East Montana, the same facility previously cited for serious conditions problems. No open bidding. No competition.
In a single recent month, ICE posted just 2 competitive contracts on SAM.gov and awarded at least 10 sole-source contracts, half justified by claiming 'only one responsible source exists.'

Federal law requires competitive bidding when the government buys goods or services above a certain threshold. It's how taxpayers get fair prices and accountability. ICE is increasingly bypassing this.
ICE has $150B+ in unspent enforcement funds and is racing to spend it by quietly bending federal procurement rules in three ways most people have never heard of. A thread.
